@base-ui/react.text: Stays, because this dashboard runs shadcn on the base-nova preset. shadcn is not tied to Base UI: components.json carries a base field of radix or base, and the shadcn package itself depends on neither -- the primitive library arrives with the components the CLI writes. Having chosen base, src/components/ui/{badge,button,separator}.tsx import it directly and removing it breaks them; card.tsx and table.tsx need no primitive at all. Switching to radix is a preset change, not a package edit. D32 first grouped it with react-aria-components as a package to remove, which was wrong -- don't re-suggest removing it.

database.text: Omitted; the dataset is too small to need one, and a local JSON file stays directly usable as context for local AI tools.

decision records.text: No ADR directory -- this file is deliberately mutable and consolidated, not a set of immutable per-decision files. Formal decisions (`D1`-`D42` below; a gap means a withdrawn decision, numbers never reused) and standalone notes live side by side, each with a stable id and a `terms` tag array for topical lookup. Tags, not a single key, since a decision usually relates to more than one term -- D26 is component-library, theme, and base-color at once, and a single key would arbitrarily pick one. Superseded reasoning is deleted in place rather than kept as annotated history; git holds what was thought before.

display-role key.text: Schema keys name how a value is displayed rather than what it means in a source domain, so a card mapper can retarget new source data onto an existing template without new code.

D1.text: The service exposes one interface; client and MCP are peers over it, not a privileged path each. Rejected: MCP reaching persistence directly, or duplicating permission logic -- either creates a second door a permission check doesn't cover. Consequence: MCP cannot run without the service process.

D2.text: `role` is a named bundle of permissions assigned to an account; `account` is the identity a caller presents. No separate developer/user concept -- what distinguishes work is which door a change goes through: dashboard configuration through the service (role-governed), built-in card mappers/packages as source-only (no role reaches them), card templates split between initialization/source and post-init assembly (`cards: write`).

D3.text: An account (credential + role name) lives in the auth store, outside dashboard data. The service resolves account, then role, then permissions, on every call. Keeps credentials and tokens out of dashboard data.

D4.text: Every request resolves to a role at one enforcement point; no caller skips it, including local callers and MCP. Rejected: role checks on agent calls only with human-trusted client endpoints -- that rebuilds the second door D1 removed.

D6.text: The application is cut into seven modules (map lives in ARCHITECTURE.md). This decision settles the cut itself: `card-templates` is separate from `contract` since templates change on a different cadence than the service surface, keeping `contract` React-free by construction.

D8.text: A card carries no position, size, or style of its own -- placement belongs to the dashboard, style is deleted as a concept (see theme, D10). Makes a card portable across dashboards, which is what makes more than one dashboard possible later. A card does carry its own state (D18).

D9.text: A dashboard is an ordered set of card references plus a theme reference -- grid-capable later, since no card claims a placement, cell/span can be added without reshaping anything. More than one dashboard over one pool of cards falls out for free, though not built yet.

D10.text: "Style" stops being a term anywhere in the project; the underlying concept -- a named set of semantic tokens whose swap changes every colour and font at once -- is theme. A dashboard carries a theme reference; theme definitions live beside it in dashboard configuration.

D11.text: A query names the integration it runs against; the two travel together, no third entity binds them. Two queries against the same integration run separately and hold their own result copies -- nothing about a query is deduplicated or pooled, except the card mapper each names (D38).

D13.text: Every write is a mutation -- a named change applied against current state, not a snapshot comparison. No revision field, no schema version, no ETag/If-Match: a queued write that replays late still applies correctly because it describes a change, not a result. Versioning earns nothing with no stored data belonging to anyone else.

D14.text: Two operations: `read(scope)` returns state, `apply(mutations)` applies one or more atomically. Mutation types are a tagged union, each carrying its required permission category, so enforcement is one lookup and the offline queue is a list of `apply` payloads. Connection authorize/disconnect is the one exception -- a live credential handoff, not a mutation, so a secret never enters the mutation or offline-queue format. Rejected: a wide RPC surface (`addCard`, `moveCard`, ...) -- each action would need its own endpoint and permission check.

D15.text: Mutations in `roles` and `integrations` require a live service; every other mutation queues offline and replays on reconnect. The line is security, not structure: a permission grant or external authorization applied blind against unseen state is the one case where "apply against whatever you find" is wrong. The client still caches for offline viewing and tells the user when offline.

D16.text: Integrations and backup targets share one module. Both are user-authorized connections to an external service; the authorization/credential-handoff code is identical and they differ only in data direction. Split later only if a second concern actually diverges.

D18.text: A card has state, updated by mutations regardless of what produced them -- no separate entity for what a card draws from, and no term for one. `{id, title, template, state}`; no card type, no manual-vs-connected distinction. State is stored already fitting the card template's schema, so rendering is a straight read.

D19.text: No mutation reaches a role -- roles join built-in card mappers and packages as source-only changes. The `roles` permission category survives read-only in effect (gates `read("roles")`); no no-widening guard is needed since nothing can widen a caller's own bundle. Settings doesn't edit roles.

D20.text: Five categories (`data`, `cards`, `presentation`, `integrations`, `roles`), each holding one ranked level (`noAccess < read < edit < write`, each implying the ones below). The split falls on the mutation, not the category -- `data: edit` alongside `cards: edit` lets a caller change what a card shows without adding or deleting cards. `edit-*` mutations never create; creation needs `write`.

D21.text: The application ships one dashboard with no create/delete mutation. It arrives in the default configuration so "no dashboard exists" is never a state the UI handles. `edit-dashboard` is the only dashboard mutation -- reorders card references, changes the theme reference.

D22.text: The service assembles a card template from a mandatory JSON Schema plus a declarative composition tree (`{component, props, children}`); the agent never writes code. Correctness comes from `tsc --noEmit` against the library's real types, not a hand-maintained parallel schema -- an earlier draft tried that and was wrong. Static trees only: no hooks, no callbacks, no drag-and-drop -- those stay hand-written. Triggers the D39 rebuild; not a hot update.

D23.text: The component library is named once at initialization, not through a mutation -- same posture as roles (D19). Fixes what a theme can say: its own CSS variables and utility classes, never arbitrary CSS, so styling stays checkable the way D22 makes composition checkable.

D24.text: Each dashboard serves its active card templates as a shadcn-compatible registry (`/r/registry.json`, `/r/<name>.json`), sourced from the active card-template manifest a build promotes (D39) -- never a directory scan, since a build has temp files and failed candidates that aren't real templates. The registry endpoint and the client view are meant to read the same active generation; as of this writing the client side does not yet (see ARCHITECTURE.md's rendering-path note -- known gap, not a design choice).

D25.text: shadcn/ui is the framework; its components and Tailwind are the defaults where this project states none of its own. A card template composes shadcn's components directly -- no headless structural layer beneath them. `react-aria-components` isn't stale as a library, just as this codebase's direction; D32 removes the reliance, and package.json confirms it's gone.

D26.text: Every colour anywhere is a semantic token from the Tailwind/shadcn set -- no hex literals, no palette-scale utilities -- which is what lets one base-colour change recolour everything instead of only what happened to be written against it. Base colour is per-user: the same card renders in different base colours for different viewers. shadcn's own preset mechanism is build-time only, so per-user base colour works by scoping token values themselves at runtime, not by re-running the CLI.

D27.text: A user's appearance -- base colour, typeset, menu colour/accent, personal presets, and which preset is selected -- lives in a file-backed store holding one record per user; secrets never live there. Base colour modifies a theme rather than sitting beside it -- it controls token values generated at init or preset-apply. A preset is a complete, literal token set in `globals-example.css` format, never a partial override. Token values are scoped per user at runtime rather than by re-running shadcn's build-time preset mechanism (D26); this entry first said generation happens only at build time, which contradicted D26 and the shipped read path. `admin` adds presets for everyone, a user may add their own ungated.

D28.text: Account credentials are hashed only (`crypto.scrypt` + `timingSafeEqual`) -- never stored, since this dashboard only ever verifies them. Integration tokens are encrypted at rest (AES-256-GCM) since they must be recoverable to send in a request. `CredentialStore` is the single seam to a stored secret. Key rotated every 90 days as a policy starting point, not a threat-model derivation; a token names the key it was sealed under so rotation needs no flag day.

D29.text: An integration (type, query surface, adapter) is shared and defined once; authorization is per-user -- two users on the same service type share one integration, not two. Queries are user-specific; results are shared once mapped into card state. Deliberate privacy posture: authorizing an integration contributes its data to a shared surface, not a private view.

D30.text: When two users' queries write the same card, the most recent write wins -- no merge, no staleness check, consistent with D13. A known ceiling, tracked with a `ponytail:` comment in the code, not a claim that conflicts don't matter. An adapter receives the relevant user's secret at update time via the existing `tokenProvider` seam. A user may only supply queries under their own identity, enforced at the one enforcement point.

D31.text: A query is private to the user who supplied it; only its result is shared (D29). A query reveals more than its result does -- whose calendar, filtered how -- so making results common was deliberate; making search terms common was not an intended side effect. Refresh runs server-side under the owner's token, so read-visibility doesn't gate whether another user's query runs.

D32.text: A query belongs to its user, never the card; only the owner (and `admin`, for deletion) reaches it. `assemble-card-template` emits a real registry item (`name`, `type`, `files`, `dependencies`, `registryDependencies`) paired with its JSON Schema, rather than a bare file the registry wraps after the fact. `react-aria-components` leaves `package.json` outright; `@base-ui/react` stays. The original five card templates (raw HTML, no styling, pre-dating every later decision) were deleted outright; their schemas were kept for tests at `src/test-support/card-template.ts`. `message` is the first shadcn replacement (#82).

D33.text: A user says what things look like in the library's own vocabulary, never in CSS, never touching a card template's markup or a card's data. `components.json` fields that change generated source (`style`, `tailwind.cssVariables`, `iconLibrary`, `rtl`, plus structural fields) are project-owned; base colour, typeset, menu colour/accent, and presets are user-owned. `fontScale` is gone -- a typeset's `--typeset-size` is the same setting with a better vocabulary.

D34.text: `components.json` becomes generated per user from a project-owned template (structural/build-time fields) plus that user's runtime choices (base colour, typeset, menu fields), replaced as a whole rather than patched. Build-time fields stay fixed after initialization; changing one means reinitializing, not a preference change.

D35.text: The matrix governs shared and server-owned things only -- a user's queries, connections, appearance, and presets are theirs by structure, no category or level gates them (card mappers are the one exception, D38). Two default roles ship as ordinary configuration, not fixed names: `admin` (write on data/cards/presentation/integrations, read on roles) and `user` (write on data, read on cards/presentation/integrations, no access to roles). Roles are edited by editing the roles file the source imports -- same trust level as editing source -- and are not part of dashboard configuration. The local OS user resolves to full permissions (equal to admin); anyone else starts with none until authenticated, proven by a token written to `.dashboard/local-user-token`, hardened per platform (chmod 0600 POSIX; icacls on Windows, since chmod there only maps to a read-only flag).

D36.text: A card template is a registry item -- shadcn's own vocabulary and shape, nothing invented. An item can carry more than one component (hook, utility, tokens, stylesheet) in the same unit; this doesn't widen the assembled path, which still can't express a hook. What an agent submits must be composition of the declared library's primitives -- raw HTML or hand-written CSS is never an accepted substitute, regardless of what the browser ultimately renders.

D37.text: Initialization generates default card templates from the declared library as a project operation, not an application-role action. After initialization, `assemble-card-template` takes `cards: write` (`admin` holds it, `user` doesn't). Hand-writing a template is a source change governed by repo access and review, entering the dashboard through the same rebuild and manifest as an assembled one -- not a second install door.

D38.text: A card mapper (Fowler's mapper) sets up a correspondence between two schemas without formatting anything; named for what it maps to, since what it maps from is any structured data, not only an API response. Mappers live in one shared store referenced by name -- two queries needing the same mapping name the same mapper rather than duplicating it. Adding one is ungated, since a user who can't write one can't render their own query at all; changing or deleting a referenced one takes `cards: write`; deleting a referenced one always fails `in-use` instead of cascading.

D39.text: The build module accepts a candidate set of registry items and schemas, validates and type-checks them, and atomically promotes manifest and client assets only on full success; failure leaves the active build untouched and returns to the caller. No hot update -- an open page keeps what it loaded, the next full reload gets the promoted build. Avoids a background-job interface, partial activation, and live module replacement.

D40.text: The catalog is file-backed and outlives any one user's connection to it. An entry carries whether it's default, recommended, or dynamic, and its availability. Disconnecting destroys a user's credential immediately; a dynamic entry with zero connections expires after a project-configured retention period (default 30 days, `integrations: write` may change it). Blocking prevents new connections and refreshes but keeps everything stored, with a persistent notice to affected users. Removing with live dependencies needs an explicit override after a high-level warning -- counts and effects only, never another user's query text, identity, or credential -- and destroys credentials but leaves queries private and merely unavailable. Expiry runs at startup and on connection change; no background scheduler.

D41.text: One store holds every user's queries: a cleartext envelope (id, owner, mapper name, card fed) plus AES-256-GCM encryption of what's actually private -- which integration, what's asked -- under a host-held key bound to the owner. Costs something real: D32's structural privacy (separate per-user stores) becomes at-rest encryption plus an access check, so this protects a stolen data directory, not the server itself. Buys a single place to answer cross-user questions: whether a mapper is still referenced, whether a catalog entry is unused, who's affected by a block or removal. Same encryption seam serves connection credentials (D28) -- same shape of problem.

D42.text: The host-held key (D41) is right for a dashboard on its owner's own machine, wrong once someone else operates the host. `SecretBox` is the seam: file-backed stays the default locally, a hosted deployment supplies a managed-secrets-backed one via deployment configuration, not a code edit. `seal`/`open` are async because some managed services never release key material and perform encryption themselves -- a sync signature would rule that shape out entirely. No provider is canonical, same posture as integrations toward the services they connect to; nothing outside composition may construct its own box.
